'''''Sanguisorba''''' is a genus of flowering plants in the family [[Rosaceae]] native to the temperate regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. The common name is '''burnet'''.

==Description==
The plants are [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]]s or small shrubs. The stems grow to {{Convert abbreviated|50-200|cm}} tall and have a cluster of basal leaves, with further leaves arranged alternately up the stem. The leaves are pinnate, {{Convert abbreviated|5-30|cm}} long, with 7–25 leaflets, the leaflets with a serrated margin. Young leaves grow from the crown in the center of the plant. The flowers are small, produced in dense clusters 5–20 mm long; each flower has four very small petals, white to red in colour.

==Ecology==
''[[Sanguisorba minor]]'' is a food plant for the larvae of the [[grizzled skipper]] (''Pyrgus malvae'') and the [[mouse moth]] (''Amphipyra tragopoginis''). The caterpillars of both the [[Scarce large blue|scarce]] and [[dusky large blue]] feed on ''[[Sanguisorba officinalis]]''.

==Cultivation and uses==
Burnets are cultivated as garden plants. Many [[cultivar]]s have been bred, especially from ''[[Sanguisorba officinalis|S. officinalis]]''. ''[[Sanguisorba canadensis|S. canadensis]]'' is grown for its white flowers on stems that well exceed a meter tall. The plants [[hybrid (biology)|hybridize]] easily, producing new mixes.<ref name=rhs>Sutton, J. [http://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/RHS-Publications/Journals/The-Plantsman/2007-issues/June/Sanguisorba ''Sanguisorba'' in Cultivation.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130828045025/http://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/RHS-Publications/Journals/The-Plantsman/2007-issues/June/Sanguisorba |date=2013-08-28 }} ''The Plantsman''. Royal Horticultural Society. June, 2007. 78-83.</ref> ''[[Sanguisorba obtusa|S. obtusa]]'' is valued for its foliage of pink-edged, gray-green leaves.<ref name=tele>Bourne, V. [https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/howtogrow/3304829/How-to-grow-sanguisorba.html How to grow: ''Sanguisorba''.] ''The Daily Telegraph'' September 21, 2002.</ref>

''Sanguisorba officinalis'' is used in traditional Chinese medicinal to treat [[gastrointestinal condition]]s and bleeding.<ref name=choi>{{cite journal |vauthors=Choi J, Kim MY, Cha BC, Yoo ES, Yoon K, Lee J, Rho HS, Kim SY, Cho JY |title=ZYM-201 sodium succinate ameliorates streptozotocin-induced hyperlipidemic conditions |journal=Planta Med. |volume=78 |issue=1 |pages=12–7 |date=January 2012 |pmid=21928167 |doi=10.1055/s-0031-1280219 |url=http://www.thieme-connect.com/DOI/DOI?10.1055/s-0031-1280219|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

''Sanguisorba minor'', salad burnet, has similarly been used medicinally in Europe to control bleeding. The leaves have a cucumber flavour and can be eaten in salads, or used fresh or dried and made into a tea.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bown |first1=Deni |title=The Royal Horticultural Society New Encyclopaedia of Herbs & Their Uses |date=2002 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley Limited |location=London |isbn=0-7513-3386-7}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The Latin genus name ''Sanguisorba'' means 'blood stauncher'. 'Sanguis' is a cognate with 'sanguine', meaning 'blood'. 'Sorbeo' means 'to staunch'. The plant is known to have [[styptic]] properties.<ref name="gledhill">{{cite book |last=Gledhill |first=David |year=2008 |title=The Names of Plants |url=https://archive.org/details/namesplants00gled_746 |url-access=limited |publisher=MCambridge University Press |isbn=9780521866453 |page=[https://archive.org/details/namesplants00gled_746/page/n348 339]}}</ref>
